To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
1. high effort/low gain conditions in occupational life are a major source of stress and 2. they are related to new cardiovascular events, hypertension and atherogenic lipid profiles.

high effort/low gain conditions, as assessed by the effort reward imbalance (ERI) model, are associated with new cardiovascular events and cardiovascular risk factors in prospective studies on blue collar men.
high effort/low control and low reward conditions are associated with adverse health effects.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following topics: (1) development of a new questionnaire for the assessment of effort reward imbalance in the occupational setting, (2) validation of the new questionnaire, and (3) testing the effort reward imbalance concept with respect to adverse health effects in prospective cohort studies.
the question of whether the effort reward imbalance concept is useful for the prediction of adverse health effects of occupational life.

the following issues: (1) the development of a new model to assess adverse health effect of high effort/ low reward conditions; (2) the assessment of psychosocial stressors in the workplace; (3) the assessment of cardiovascular risk factors; (4) the assessment of new cardiovascular events; and (5) the assessment of the association of stressors, cardiovascular risk factors, new cardiovascular events.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
high effort/low control conditions are particularly harmful to health, whereas low effort/high reward conditions are particularly beneficial.
the demand control model is a good model for the study of cardiovascular disease.
high effort/low gain conditions at work are a risk factor for adverse health effects, in particular cardiovascular events.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
high effort/low gain conditions at work are associated with adverse health effects in terms of cardiovascular disease.

effort reward imbalance may be considered as an important risk factor for cardiovascular disease and that this risk factor is independent of the well known risk factors such as hypertension or hypercholesterolemia.
the effort reward imbalance concept is a useful addition to the person/environment fit model and to the demand control model.
The main takeaway from our work is that
effort reward imbalance is a new and important risk factor for adverse health outcomes.
high effort/low control conditions are associated with adverse health effects in terms of cardiovascular risk factors, new cardiovascular events, and mortality.
the effort-reward imbalance model is a valid and useful tool for understanding and predicting health effects of work stress.
